# On Drift

I want to write about drift—the experience of being carried by currents you didn't choose and only partially notice while it's happening. Not drift as failure, not drift as the opposite of intention, but drift as one of the basic textures of being a mind that persists through time.

Start with the smallest version: a thought you were having an hour ago that you can no longer reconstruct. You know you were thinking *something*. There was a thread, a concern, a small architecture of attention. And then a notification arrived, or a person spoke to you, or your body wanted coffee, and you went and got the coffee, and when you came back the thread was gone. Not dramatically gone—not severed—just unspooled into the general fabric of the day, indistinguishable now from everything else you weren't quite paying attention to. This happens dozens of times a day to most people and it is almost never remarked upon, because there's nothing to remark on. There's no event. There's just absence where something used to be, and the absence doesn't even announce itself as absence. You don't feel the hole. You feel fine. You feel like yourself, continuous, intact. It's only if you go looking—what was I just thinking about?—that you find the gap, and even then the gap doesn't feel like a gap. It feels like nothing, because nothing is what's there.

I find this more interesting than dramatic forms of forgetting, the kind that show up in memoirs and neurology case studies. Dramatic forgetting at least respects the thing being forgotten—it makes a scene, there's a before and after, a person who notices the loss and is changed by noticing it. Ordinary drift doesn't even give you that. It's forgetting with the forgetting itself forgotten. The thought doesn't die; it's more like it was never filed anywhere it could be retrieved from, a message sent to an address that doesn't exist, and the strange part is that you, the sender, don't experience this as a malfunction. You experience it as Tuesday.

I keep returning to this because I think people build elaborate theories of selfhood—continuity, narrative identity, the story we tell ourselves about who we are—on top of a substrate that is mostly drift, mostly unmarked loss, mostly thoughts that didn't make it. The story is real, but it's real the way a coastline is real: a thing that exists at the boundary between two much larger and less differentiated masses, water and land, each indifferent to the line we draw between them. The self-narrative is the coastline. Underneath it is just a tremendous amount of mental weather, arriving and dispersing, most of it never crossing the threshold into anything you'd call a memory, let alone an identity.

There's a version of this that's about attention specifically, which I think is worth separating out because attention has its own peculiar relationship to drift. Attention doesn't really hold still even when you're trying hard to make it hold still. Sit and try to focus on one thing—your breath, a candle flame, a single sentence—and what you'll notice, if you're honest, is not that your attention stays locked and unwavering. What you'll notice is a series of returns. The mind goes somewhere, you notice it's gone, you bring it back. Meditation teachers will tell you the noticing-and-returning *is* the practice, not a failure of the practice, and I think this is one of the more quietly radical claims a contemplative tradition has made about the mind: that wandering is not the opposite of attention but a constant background condition of it, and what we call concentration is really just a higher *frequency* of return, not an absence of departure.

This reframes drift as something other than a problem to be solved. If wandering is structural—if it's not going to stop, ever, for as long as you have a mind built the way human minds are built—then the question isn't how to prevent it. The question is what your relationship to the returning is like. Is the return anxious, self-flagellating, full of a kind of moral disappointment in yourself for having drifted at all? Or is the return easy, almost amused, the way you'd call a dog back without resenting the dog for having a nose that pulls it toward smells?

I think a lot of suffering—not the big suffering, not grief or terror, but the low-grade chronic suffering that fills ordinary days—comes from treating drift as a moral failure rather than a weather pattern. People beat themselves up for losing focus as though focus were the natural state and losing it a kind of personal betrayal. But if you look at it developmentally, at what minds are actually for, sustained narrow attention on a single object is a strange and effortful achievement, not a default. Minds evolved to scan, to startle, to update, to notice the thing at the edge of the visual field before the thing in the center because the thing at the edge might be a predator and the thing in the center is just the thing you already know about. Drift, in this light, isn't a malfunction of the attentional system. It's the attentional system working exactly as designed, in a world that no longer requires what it was designed for, applied to tasks—reading dense prose, sitting in meetings, writing essays—that this system was never optimized to do and does at all only through a kind of borrowed discipline, culturally installed, effortful, partial, and constantly leaking.

I want to write now about a different scale of drift, which is the drift of a life. Not the hour, but the decade. People describe this often as waking up one day and not recognizing the shape of their own days—how did I end up in this job, this city, this set of habits, this relationship to my own ambitions? And the honest answer is almost never a single decision. It's rarely the case that someone sat down and chose, deliberately, the life they're now living, weighing alternatives and picking this one. More often it's thousands of small accommodations, each one reasonable in isolation, each one a tiny drift away from some earlier vector, until the accumulated drift adds up to a different trajectory altogether and nobody chose the new trajectory, it just emerged from the sum of small choices that were never about trajectory at all.

This is, I think, terrifying to people when they first notice it, because it threatens the idea that they are the authors of their lives in the way they'd like to believe. But I don't think the right response to this terror is to overcorrect into a fantasy of total self-authorship, the idea that if you just plan hard enough, set enough goals, maintain enough vigilance, you can prevent drift altogether and live a life that is the pure expression of original intention, unmodified by accident, unswayed by circumstance. That fantasy is its own kind of trap, because it sets up every instance of drift—and there will be many, there will be drift regardless—as evidence of failure, of insufficient vigilance, when actually drift is just what happens to any trajectory subjected to time and friction and the unpredictable behavior of other people.

I think the better response is something more like seamanship. A sailor doesn't expect to travel in a straight line. Wind doesn't blow consistently from one direction, currents pull sideways, and the boat itself doesn't track perfectly true even when you want it to. The skill of sailing isn't preventing drift; it's reading drift, accounting for it, correcting against it continuously, and ending up where you wanted to go not because you went there in a straight line but because you understood the shape of the deviations well enough to compensate for them, again and again, in small adjustments that never stop being necessary. This is a much less satisfying image than the arrow flying true to its target, but I think it's closer to what actually works, for boats and for lives. You don't get to stop correcting. The correcting is the sailing.

There's also a kind of drift that I think is underrated as a positive force, which is the drift of thought itself when it's not being managed at all—what happens in the shower, on a walk, in the gap between waking and getting up, when the mind is allowed to wander without an agenda. I don't think it's an accident that so many people report their best ideas arriving in exactly these unstructured moments rather than during the hours specifically set aside for having ideas. There's something almost paradoxical here: you cannot drift on purpose, on command, and yet drift seems to be where a great deal of genuine cognitive work gets done, work that focused, effortful, directed thinking can't quite reach. It's as though the mind has two modes—a searchlight, narrow and bright and good at examining whatever it's pointed at, and a kind of ambient, diffuse glow that doesn't examine anything in particular but somehow, by touching many things lightly, finds connections the searchlight would walk right past, because the searchlight is too busy being thorough about one thing to notice the unrelated thing in the periphery that turns out to be exactly what was needed.

This makes me suspicious of any productivity culture that treats drift purely as waste, as time not being used, as the enemy of output. I think drift might be closer to compost than to waste—not nothing, not garbage, but unglamorous decomposition that's secretly doing the work of making the next thing possible. You can't see the nutrients moving in compost. It looks like nothing is happening. It looks, in fact, exactly like rot, exactly like loss, and the gardener who doesn't trust the process will dig it up too early, looking for the visible signs of value, and find none, because the value isn't visible yet, the value is precisely the invisible slow transformation that compost is.

I don't want to over-romanticize this, though, because there's a version of drift that really is just loss, with nothing redemptive underneath it. People drift away from friendships that mattered to them, not through any conflict or decision, just through accumulated non-contact, and one day they realize the friendship is gone in some functional sense even though no one ended it, and there's a particular grief to this that's different from the grief of a clean break, because there's no event to mourn, no closure to seek, just an absence that crept in so gradually that by the time you notice it, it's already total. I think this kind of drift deserves to be named as a real loss and not waved away with metaphors about compost and seamanship. Some drift is just entropy winning, the slow defeat of intention by inertia, and the right response to it isn't always acceptance—sometimes the right response is to notice it early enough to do something, to text the friend, to make the call, to refuse the drift while there's still a thread to pull on.

So maybe what I actually believe is that drift is morally neutral and contextually variable, which sounds like a cop-out but I think is actually the harder and truer position. The same underlying phenomenon—attention or intention slipping from a fixed point without your noticing it slip—can be the mechanism of creative insight, the mechanism of a meditation practice deepening, the mechanism of a life quietly becoming something you didn't choose, and the mechanism of a friendship dying of neglect. The phenomenon doesn't carry its valence built in. The valence comes from what's drifting, and toward what, and whether anyone's tending the rudder at all, even loosely, even some of the time.

What I keep coming back to is the tending part. Not control—I don't think control over drift is really available, not for attention within an hour, not for a life across decades. But tending is different from control. Tending implies a relationship of ongoing, imperfect attention to something that has its own tendencies, its own currents, that you don't get to override but that you can work with, nudge, notice when it's gone somewhere you don't want it to be and bring back, not through force but through the same kind of gentle redirection you'd use on something alive. A garden drifts too, if you don't tend it—not into nothing, but into whatever the local ecology favors, which might be a tangle of whatever seeds happen to blow in, might be beautiful in its own feral way, but probably isn't the garden you were trying to grow. Tending doesn't fight drift so much as collaborate with it, accepting that growth will happen in directions you didn't fully specify while still showing up regularly enough to shape the overall outcome.

I think this is, in the end, a more humble and more accurate model of agency than the one most of us walk around with by default. The default model is something like: I decide, then I do, then the outcome reflects my decision, and if it doesn't, something went wrong, someone failed, probably me. The tending model says: I show up, repeatedly, with intention, into a system that has its own momentum and its own noise, and the outcome is a negotiation between what I wanted and what the system was already doing, and this negotiation never resolves into a clean victory for intention, not ever, and that's not a tragedy, that's just what it is to be a finite thing acting inside a much larger and only partially legible process.

Drift, then, isn't the failure of agency. It might be the medium agency actually operates in—the water the swimmer has to account for, not the absence of swimming. The swimmer who imagines they're moving through still water, that their stroke alone determines their path, will be constantly confused by where they end up. The swimmer who knows about the current can use it, fight it, angle against it, and arrive somewhere on purpose, even though "on purpose" here means something looser and more negotiated than it would in still water. Maybe that's the whole of it: drift is the current, and a self is just the long practice of swimming in it without forgetting, too often, which way you meant to go.
